tn.quote: Dermuha has four tones: high, mid, low and high-glottal. The high-glottal is relatively rare in the data compared to the other tones. The high tone is indicated by /˥/, the mid tone by /˧/, the low tone by /˩/ and the high glottal tone by /˥ˀ/. The high tone /˥/ starts at a high pitch but is slightly lower at the end. The high glottal /˥ˀ/ begins at a high pitch but falls slightly to low at the end and ends abruptly. The mid tone /˧/ is mid in pitch and vaguely drops at the end. The low tone /˩/ begins slightly lower than the mid tone and not dramatically falls to low at the end.

4269.tone: The source treats Mocho' as a final-stress language with an incipient tonal contrast parasitic on stress: long vowels are plain or have falling pitch, and 'Falling pitch is only found in syllables in stressed position and is neutralized in any other position' (Sec. 2.3.3, p. 38); the contrast is 'only found in nominals' since the verbal formative suffix neutralizes it. Stress correlates: peak (high) pitch of the word on stressed short/plain long vowels, falling pitch on marked long vowels; intensity and length are weak correlates. Sec. 1.6: 'long vowels also have contrastive pitch in stressed syllables.' Not a tone system with no stress rule; the stress rule is explicit, so fixed and quantity-insensitive rather than tone or pitch accent.

4270.qtr: I further note that, although in writing there is very much agreement between these languages, in speech very much difference exists. In the first place the different placing of the stress contributes to this. Galela, for example, never changes the stress by the addition of suffixes; Tobelo shifts the stress precisely onto the suffix; Madole pronounces the exponents o, ma, etc. as if these were an integral part of the word and gives those the stress, etc. To the ear there is quite a lot of difference between these languages, so that people do not understand one another in either direction.

4270.prule: No stress-placement rule stated. 4271.dq: L'accent et le schème tonal caractérisent également le mot phonologique mais sans lui conférer des limites aussi opératoires que le trait de palatalisation. Une syllabe finale est toujours accentuée devant pause (externe ou interne) (p. 445) ... Toute syllabe devant pause (interne ou externe) est accentuée ce qui entraîne la même règle d'épenthèse pausale (p. 456)
4271.dloc: Livre 1, chapter 'Le mot phonologique': §2.1 Les frontières externes, p. 445; verbal complex p. 451; §4 Conclusion p. 456. Tonal accent: §4.7 'Schèmes tonals structurels: schèmes accentuels' pp. 365-366 and §8.4 p. 426.
4271.heavy: Not applicable: the pausal accent is explicitly quantity-insensitive ('sur la syllabe finale, ouverte ou fermée'); the lexical prominence is tonal.
4271.prule: Two-tone language (registers H and B, only H marked). Each basic, non-derived word carries at most one H tone, which Barreteau reinterprets as a lexically placed 'accent tonal': absent (BB, BBB), initial (HB, HBB), internal (BHB) or final (BH, BBH), i.e. a pitch-accent-style analysis of lexical tone, not a stress rule. Separately, a non-distinctive 'accent d'intensité' falls automatically on the final syllable (open or closed) of the phonological word before a pause, external or internal.
4271.srule: Only in reduplicated words: the simple (non-derived) phonological word has a single, non-distinctive intensity accent on its final syllable before pause; in adjectivo-adverbals and nouns derived by full or partial reduplication, the final syllable of each reduplicated part before the internal (virtual or semi-) pause is also accented (daf-daf-dafaf 'épais'), the internal accent disappearing in rapid speech; prefix mV- and initial CV- reduplication take no pause. No primary/secondary ranking and no rhythmic stress is described.
4271.quote: Une syllabe finale est toujours accentuée devant pause (externe ou interne): elle est prononcée avec plus de force et surtout, elle est toujours vocalisée, qu'elle se termine par une syllabe ouverte: (C)CV, ou fermée: (C)CVC. C'est ainsi que nous analysons les syllabes finales (C)CVC comme des réalisations pausales accentuées de (C)CC avec épenthèse. La position de l'accent d'intensité est fixe et systématique devant pause; il n'est donc pas distinctif. (p. 445) ... Devant pause, un accent d'intensité se porte automatiquement sur la syllabe finale, ouverte ou fermée, ce qui entraîne la règle …
4271.loc: Livre 1, chapter 'Le mot phonologique': §2.1 Les frontières externes, p. 445; verbal complex p. 451; §4 Conclusion p. 456. Tonal accent: §4.7 'Schèmes tonals structurels: schèmes accentuels' pp. 365-366 and §8.4 p. 426.

Nous avons effectué un autre séjour au Cameroun, de 1979 à 1981.'…
4271.exq_: La position de l'accent d'intensité est fixe et systématique devant pause; il n'est donc pas distinctif. (p. 445)
4271.tone: Two tone registers H and B, only H marked (p. 353). Basic words carry at most one H, reinterpreted as an 'accent tonal' (pp. 365-366, 426); H entails vowel tension. The 1983 thesis §4.2-4.3 (pp. 374-376) formalises [+haut] -> [+accent] and states 'il conviendrait de distinguer deux types d'accent: l'accent tonal et l'accent d'intensité, l'accent tonal impliquant celui d'intensité mais non pas l'inverse'; §4.1 (p. 373): 'Les syllabes finales de mot (ouvertes ou fermées) sont toujours accentuées devant pause... quel que soit le ton de celle-ci.' Hollingsworth 1980 p. 1: Mofu-Gudur 'is a tonal language which also exhibits stress'; p. 9: 'while a tonal language, also has stress which influences the tone on the word, phrase, and sentence levels. On an utterance in a discourse stress is frequently predictable on the basis of grammatical criteria' -- his 'stress' is speaker-assigned information focus (super-high pitch), not a word-level position.

4274.dq: Pada akhir kata, kadang-kadang terdapat vokal yang panjang, dan vokal itulah yang ditekankan. ... Bahasa Moma memiliki beberapa enklitik ... yang diucapkan sama seperti akhiran tetapi tidak mempengaruhi ucapan kata dasarnya. ... Suku kata yang tebal ditekankan.
4274.dloc: 'Petunjuk' (Ejaan Percobaan Bahasa Moma-Kulawi): p. x, paragraph 'VOKAL PANJANG'; p. xi, paragraph 'LAIPEKUNEMU'I' (enclitics); 'Pololita Eo-eona / Percakapan Sehari-hari', note p. 249 (pp. 14, 15, 269).
4274.heavy: A long vowel at the end of the word ('Pada akhir kata, kadang-kadang terdapat vokal yang panjang, dan vokal itulah yang ditekankan'), written with two vowel letters: hamaa, paletaa, toronaa, humpii, woo, mpuu. The source adds only that long vowels do not occur at the beginning of a word ('Vokal panjang tidak terdapat pada awal kata panjang'); it does not say they are absent non-finally, and its own stress marking shows base-final long vowels before enclitics inside the written word, all carrying the stress (para[luu]ku, para[luu]ta, para[luu]mu, para[luu]kudi, [wuu]ku, po’o[haa]ta, Natoro[naa]’adapa), so 'end of the word' means the end of the word minus enclitics. The bold marking also treats final diphthongs as one stressed unit ([hou], [rau], tu[mai], We[lau], Na[bai], [hei], [ei]).
4274.dflt: Penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes, excluding enclitics. Not stated in prose in the open source; established by the source's own stress marking (independent tally over 286 bold-marked Moma tokens in pp. 249-263: 170 penult of the written word, 60 penult of the base once an enclitic string is set aside, 27 'final' = final long vowel/diphthong units, monosyllables and I[yo], 29 residue that are mostly enclitic-stripping misses of the crude script, e.g. Me[ha]nitamo, tu[a]kaku, ro[du]amo; the compilers tally with hand-checked enclitics gives 298/304 penult) and stated in words second-hand by Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 (Google Books): 'prominence is associated with the penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes but excluding pronominal and adverbial clitics. Enclitics do not attract prominence even when they are disyllabic, as in ['hou=kami]' citing Adriani & Esser 1939: 9.
4274.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, counting suffixes but not enclitics; a long vowel (written VV) at the end of the word minus enclitics, or a final diphthong, is itself stressed. Equivalently: stress on the penultimate mora of the word minus enclitics.

4275.dq: On non-monosyllabic words only two levels are contrastive, and these on the stressed syllable only.
4275.dloc: Endnote 1, pp. 201-202; also p. 187 examples (6)-(7) for tone marks on polysyllables
4275.prule: No stress-placement rule stated. Momuna is described as a tone language: three contrastive tone levels (high, mid, low) on monosyllables; on polysyllabic words a two-way tone contrast carried by the stressed syllable only. The note presupposes one stressed syllable per polysyllabic word but never says where it falls or whether its position is predictable.
4275.quote: Momuna phonemes are orthographically symbolised as follows: the stops t, k, b; the liquid r; the sibilant s; the nasals m, n; the semi-vowels w, y; the labialised stops bw, kw; the palatalised consonants sy, by, ny; the vowels i, ee (close mid front), e (open mid front), a, o (low back), oo (close mid back), u; the diphthongs ei, ai, oi, au, ou. There are three levels of contrastive tone on monosyllables: high (marked by the acute accent), mid (unmarked) and low (marked by a grave accent). On non-monosyllabic words only two levels are contrastive, and these on the stressed syllable only.
4275.loc: Endnote 1, pp. 201-202; also p. 187 examples (6)-(7) for tone marks on polysyllables
4275.idn: Momuna (originally called 'Somahai'), Papuan language spoken between the Balim and Kolff River systems, Kabupaten Jayawijaya, Irian Jaya (Indonesia); data: Note 1, p. 202: 'The present study was undertaken in a workshop held in 1984 in Danau Bira, Irian Jaya with the Cooperative Program of Cenderawasih University and…
4275.tone: Three contrastive tone levels on monosyllables (high = acute, mid = unmarked, low = grave); on polysyllables only two levels contrast, and only on the stressed syllable, i.e. tone contrast is culminative on the stressed syllable (compatible with a pitch-accent-type analysis, but Reimer calls it tone and gives no stress rule). The text examples mark tone on polysyllables: p. 187 ex. (6) 'Máenee', 'Rúenee' (acute on the first vowel of both names) and ex. (7) 'kì' (grave on a monosyllable); two proper names are too few to read a placement pattern off. Usher (New Guinea World, second-hand from Reimer 1986 and an unpublished Reimer n.d. phonology) restates it as two tones 'on the vowel which carries primary stress' and notes that Reimer's materials mark high and low tones on disyllables without explanation.

4278.heavy: A syllable containing a two-vowel cluster /VV/ (/ii yy uu ee aa oo yi ui ei ai oi/), each /V/ counted separately in the right-to-left count (condition 107c(1) 'a single /V/ (not /VV/)' confirms /VV/ syllables are the heavy class); and the word-final syllable when the word ends in /C/. A medial syllable closed by /h/ or /ʔ/ is not heavy (e.g. /wah/ in /,suwah,kwinunu'hihti./ is unstressed while /su/ is stressed).
4278.dflt: V-final all-light words: penult, then every second syllable leftward (4 syllables 1010; 5 syllables 01010 with weak stress on the initial syllable; a 10010 unit only under the 107c conditions); C-final all-light words: final syllable. Stress is never on the antepenult with both following syllables unstressed.
4278.prule: Right-edge mora count. In a V-final word the stressed syllable is the one containing the next-to-last /V/: the penult when the last two syllables are CV, but a final syllable with a /VV/ cluster (long vowel or diphthong, counted as two /V/) takes the stress itself; in a C-final word the final syllable is stressed. Word-level primary = this rightmost computed stress; it becomes 'strong' stress only when it is the last stressed syllable before the intonational juncture /./ (i.e. in isolation or phrase-finally), otherwise it is 'intermediate'.
4278.srule: Iterative right-to-left by vowel count from the primary stress: the syllable containing the second /V/ before a stressed syllable is stressed, and so on leftward (each /V/ of a /VV/ cluster counts, so CV syllables alternate and a CVV syllable next to a stress is itself stressed); these are 'intermediate' stresses (§107d); an initial syllable not reached by the count has 'weak' stress (§107b); under four segmental conditions (§107c) a stress stands on the third syllable before a stressed one, never at the word end.

tn.translation: Tonic accent. — The tonic accent consists in a 'stroke of the voice' without perceptible raising of pitch. The syllable bearing it is pronounced with more intensity or effort. It ordinarily falls on the first syllable not marked with the sign of shortness. Pitch accent. — The pitch accent consists in a raising of pitch, either on a monosyllabic word or on one or several syllables of the same word. It is indicated by an acute accent placed on the accented syllable.

4282.prule: CONFLICT between reachable first-hand descriptions. Hofling 2011: lexical stress on the first syllable of the root and on alternate syllables from there; every syllable with a long (CVVC) or glottalized (CV'[V]C) vowel is stressed; phrase-final echo vowels unstressed. Against this, three earlier first-hand descriptions put primary stress on the last syllable of the word: Schumann Gálvez 1997 (non-phonemic, two degrees; monosyllables primary; disyllables secondary on the first syllable and primary on the last; trisyllables 'por lo general' primary on the last and secondary on the first: 21 janal, 21 nojbej), Verbeeck 1998 ('As a rule Mopan primary stress falls on the last syllable of the word'; 'Stress on the final syllable of words in isolation'), Ulrich & Ulrich 1982 ('Stress occurs typically on the ultimate syllable'). Root-initial and word-final primary stress cannot both hold for a plain disyllabic root.
4282.srule: Conflicting, like the primary rule. Schumann Gálvez 1997 (final-stress side): two degrees of stress; disyllables and, 'por lo general', trisyllables carry secondary stress on the FIRST syllable and primary on the last (21 janal 'comida', 21 nojbej 'camino principal'); monosyllables primary only. Hofling 2011 (root-initial side): stress on the root-initial syllable and on alternate syllables counted from it, plus every syllable with a long (CVVC) or glottalized (CV'[V]C) vowel; primary vs secondary not ranked. Not mentioned in the reachable text of Verbeeck 1998 (sec. 5.1.4) or Ulrich & Ulrich 1982 (fn. 2) / 1976 ('El acento').

Where placement is predictable (the general case for roots), the accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the root: exx. 116-121 óko, éra, yú.a, déci, éyrir, éfej, óduy, edíder, mahína, oysúra, ofóga; monosyllabic roots accented (már, ég, ní). 4288.srule: None in simplex words: 'only one fixed accent per polysyllabic word' (p. 51), other syllables low or neutral (p. 49); no rhythmic or alternating accent is described; prefixes, circumfix, enclitic -o and paragogic -a are unaccented and mos- compounds keep a single accent on the noun root (p. 102), as do lexicalized compounds (p. 105); ordinary noun compounds are said to carry an accent on both roots (§3.1.4 p. 99). 4288.tone: The source classifies Moskona explicitly as a pitch-accent language (§1.3.2 p. 8 'the prosodic system is pitch accent'; §2.3 p. 49; Appendix A p. 409 'pitch accent languages with only one tone melody'), of the culminative type: a single tonal contrast, high tone on the one accented syllable per word, other syllables low or neutral, 'the accent functioning like the main stress in a stress system'. Contrasted with the lexical-tone languages Abun and Mpur and the stress languages Hatam (metrical stress) and Maybrat (lexical stress) in the same area (p. 49). Acoustic correlates (§2.3.1 pp. 50-51): pitch change is the main component, with greater amplitude and usually greater duration, but the pitch difference can be as small as 0.6 semitones with amplitude the stronger cue, and duration 'does not always correlate with accent'. Accented syllables are written with an acute accent; in chapters after ch. 2 only roots with unpredictable accent are marked (p. 49).

tn.quote: Le mooré est une langue à ton ponctuel. ... L’unité porteuse de ton en mooré est la syllabe. ... Cependant, Peterson (1971) et Kinda (1984) distinguent deux tons pertinents en mooré, mais qui sont réalisés en trois tons. ... Il y a en fait un phénomène de surface, l’abaissement tonal (downstep), qui se produit en mooré. C’est ce phénomène qui est perçu comme le troisième ton réalisé dans la structure de surface. ... tn.translation: Mooré is a level-tone (register-tone) language. ... The tone-bearing unit in Mooré is the syllable. ... However, Peterson (1971) and Kinda (1984) distinguish two relevant tones in Mooré, which are realised as three tones. ... There is in fact a surface phenomenon, tonal lowering (downstep), which occurs in Mooré. It is this phenomenon that is perceived as the third tone realised in the surface structure. ... Thus Mooré has only two tones, which have three levels of realisation. Platiel and Kaboré (1998) likewise establish two level tones in Mooré.

'A note on the tones of Moyon' (in Rajapurohit ed., Acoustic Studies in Indian Languages, CIIL Mysore, pp. 107-108; read from the archive.org DLI scan, pp. 130-131): 'Like the other neighbouring Tibeto-Burman languages, Moyon is also a tonal language. A word can have different meanings with different tones, which are three in number' (high rising, low, high level, e.g. [tfa] 'cry after' / 'be good' / 'mourn'); the only mention of stress is 'Similarly a change of tone or stress in a word, can give different shades of meaning with different degrees of feeling', illustrated by pitch on the last syllable of [inunseve] 'it was enjoyable' with degrees of enjoyment: expressive pitch, no placement rule. The two sources disagree on the tone inventory (two vs three tones) but agree that the word-level prosodic system is tonal and neither states a stress position.

4292.prule: No source states a word-stress rule. The language is described as a tone language: Allison 2012 (primary, open) gives five surface tones on words (L, M, H, F, R), tone 'both lexical and grammatical', functional load 'not heavy', no conditioning by consonant, vowel quality or syllable structure; earlier work (Tourneux 2000, Adam 2005) analyses two underlying registers H/B. The only stress/accent statement is Tourneux's (2021) explicitly tentative reanalysis, in a book review, of Allison's phonemic M tone as an 'accent' on a L- or H-toned syllable (B/H accented -> surface M), lexically placed (near-minimal pairs wò 'village' vs 'wò = SA wō 'summit'; gà 'mouth' vs 'gà = gā 'portion'; mɓì 'oil' vs m̀'ɓì = mɓī 'flour') and 'of very weak distinctive value today'. No position, weight or syllable-count rule is given or derivable; the accent in his table can fall on the first or a later syllable.

4292.tone: Allison 2012 p. 26: 'Makary Kotoko has five tones that appear on words: Low (unmarked: a), Mid (marked with a macron: ā), High (marked with an acute accent: á), Falling (â), Rising (ǎ).' p. 27: 'Tone does not appear to be affected by (i) contiguous consonants [...], (ii) the quality of the vowel on which the tone is realized, or (iii) the structure of the syllable in which the tone occurs.' 'Tone is both lexical and grammatical.' p. 38: 'Tone functions both lexically and grammatically in the language though the functional load of tone is not heavy.' 2.5.1: 'Both Mahamat (2005:23,187) and Tourneux (2000a) analyze Makary Kotoko as having two underlying tones.' Texts appendix: 'In natural discourse M tone is generally heard as H relative to L, and L relative to H.' The words stress/accent/prominence never occur in a stress sense in the 631-page text (a full-text search: 'stress' only in 'distress'; 'accent' only as diacritic names; 'intensity' only for reduplication/adverbs). Allison 2006 orthography statement (open, the Internet Archive copy) sect. 4 'Ton' pp. 6-7: four surface tones H, B, M, T; no stress statement. Tourneux 2021 rejects the phonemic M tone and proposes that M realisations reflect an 'accent' (syllabe accentuée) on a L- or H-toned syllable with very weak distinctive value; the phonetic nature of this accent (pitch raising vs intensity) is not stated.
